summary.text: Counting is the process of finding how many elements a finite set has, which means finding the size of the set.
The traditional method raises a counter by one for each element and marks every element visited, so none is counted twice.
Evidence suggests humans have counted for at least 50,000 years, and counting led to numeral systems and writing.

facts.label: Oldest evidence
facts.value: Humans have likely counted for at least 50,000 years

facts.label: Early uses
facts.value: Tracking group members, prey animals, property or debts

facts.label: Finger binary
facts.value: Ten fingers can reach a count of 1023

facts.label: Inclusive counting
facts.value: Always gives a count one higher than exclusive counting

facts.label: Learning to count
facts.value: From age two, children gradually learn the ordered number words

items.prompt: You want to count the cars passing your window over a whole afternoon, a small set counted over time. Which method fits?

options.label: Say numbers aloud and trust yourself to remember where you stopped
Wait until evening and estimate the total from memory
Make one stroke per car, then count all the strokes at the end
Count only the cars that happen to be in front of you now

items.explain: Making a mark for each item and counting the marks at the end works well for a small set counted over time. Spoken counting must be resumed after an interruption from a number you have to remember.

items.prompt: In English, which counts exclusively, a friend says "see you eight days from Sunday". Which day do you meet?

options.label: The Sunday one week later
The Monday one week later
The Saturday after that Sunday
The Tuesday after that Sunday

items.explain: Counting exclusively, Monday is day 1, so the following Monday is day 8. Counting inclusively, with Sunday as day 1, the following Sunday would be day 8.

items.prompt: Ana counts the starting day itself as day 1. Ben counts only at the end of each interval, so he skips the starting day. They count the same stretch of days. How do their totals compare?

options.label: Ana's total is always one higher than Ben's
Ben's total is always one higher than Ana's
Their totals are always exactly equal
Ana's total is always twice Ben's

items.explain: Inclusive counting includes the starting point and exclusive counting does not, so the inclusive count is always one greater for the same set.

items.prompt: A musician says two notes form a "third". Counting as music does, how many notes up from the starting note is that?

options.label: Three notes up
One note up
Four notes up
Two notes up

items.explain: Music counts intervals inclusively: going up one note is a second and going up two notes is a third.

items.prompt: A teacher gives every student in a class a different number so that each one can be picked out individually. Which term fits this?

options.label: Enumeration
Exclusive counting
Tallying
Verbal counting

items.explain: Enumeration means uniquely identifying each element of a set by assigning it a number.

items.prompt: A toddler recites "one, two, three, four" smoothly. Can you conclude they understand what each number word means?

options.label: Yes, a smooth recital proves the meanings are understood
Yes, but only if they use their fingers while reciting
Not necessarily, since they may only know the word sequence
No, children cannot learn number words before school

items.explain: Children learn the ordered sequence of number words gradually, and may say it without understanding what the individual words mean.
